1. PREMISE: Your framing treats boundary-setting as a problem of managing social warmth while preserving friendliness—a false choice. The hidden assumption is that reducing participation in collective disparagement requires you to maintain the same interpersonal temperature with these four people. The entire analysis turns on recognizing that boundary-setting means changing your behavior unilaterally, not negotiating a joint recalibration of the relationship.

2. STAKES: The four senior staff members stand to lose regular participation in their established social ritual and lose confirmation of shared grievances from a younger colleague they have incorporated into their circle. New staff members stand to gain protection from having their character assessed in your presence and your absence from conversations that damage their standing in the workplace. Management stands to gain information asymmetry advantage—they will not know the full scope of organized discontent. You stand to gain clarity about your own professional judgment, reduced complicity in decisions you later regret, and protection against being identified as part of a faction if workplace conflict escalates. Your own learning and task completion stand to recover time currently spent in these conversations.

3. DIRECTIVE: Cease participating in assessments of other staff members' character or competence immediately and permanently. Your participation signals that these evaluations constitute legitimate workplace discourse and binds you to a faction whose interests may diverge from yours.
[Rejected path: Continue joining these conversations while gradually reducing frequency. This produces a slow exit that leaves you partially compromised for months, allows the four staff members to believe you may re-engage, and creates ambiguity about whether you stand behind prior statements you made—probability of primary harm: high.]

4. RECOMMENDATION: Stop speaking negatively about colleagues in your workplace at once. Exclusion from this ritual will more reliably secure your professional autonomy than gradual withdrawal, because it forces the four senior staff members to adjust their expectations of you immediately rather than treat you as temporarily unavailable. The competing claim—that abrupt change will damage relationships—assumes these relationships depend on your participation in collective disparagement; they do not, and relationships that require this participation are built on mutual vulnerability rather than mutual respect. Therefore: Redirect conversation to work topics whenever assessments of other staff arise, and answer questions about your weekend or personal life with factual brevity rather than invitation.
